alt: Accelerator with capital-output ratio 3: induced investment is 30 in year 2 when output rises by 10, falls to 12 in year 3 when output rises by only 4, is zero in year 4 when output is unchanged and recovers to 18 in year 5 when output rises by 6.
caption: Figure: investment responds to the change in output, so it falls even while output is still rising (year 3) and is zero when output is flat (year 4)

alt: Stagflation in AD/AS: an oil price rise shifts SRAS left by 1,100 at every price level from SRAS1 to SRAS2; the equilibrium moves from price level 110 and output 10,600 to price level 120 and output 10,000, so the price level rises while real output and employment fall (cost-push).
caption: Figure: a fall in SRAS raises the price level (110 to 120) and lowers real output (10,600 to 10,000): stagflation

alt: AD/AS with the worked schedule: AD1 and SRAS meet at a price level of 110 and real output 10,600, below potential output 12,000 (vertical LRAS); AD rises by 1,100 at every price to AD2, giving a new equilibrium at price level 120 and output 11,100, so both output and the price level rise (demand-pull).
caption: Figure: an increase in AD raises both real output (10,600 to 11,100) and the price level (110 to 120); the economy stays below potential output of 12,000

alt: Aggregate demand schedule: on AD1 a rise in the price level from 100 to 110 moves along the curve from 11,000 to 10,400; a non-price cause such as higher confidence shifts the whole curve right by 1,000 to AD2, so real demand at a price level of 100 rises from 11,000 to 12,000.
caption: Figure: a change in the price level moves along AD1; any other cause shifts the whole curve to AD2 (1,000 more at each price level)

alt: A buffer stock with a floor of US$35 and a ceiling of US$45: in a good harvest the market price would be US$32, so at US$35 the agency buys the 60 tonnes by which supply of 310 exceeds demand of 250; in a poor harvest the price would be US$48, so at US$45 it sells 60 tonnes from stock to meet demand of 150 against supply of 90.
caption: Figure: the agency buys 60 tonnes in a good harvest (green) and sells 60 in a poor one (red) to hold price between US$35 and US$45

alt: Actual and potential real GDP over six years: potential grows steadily from 1,000 to 1,160 while actual output crosses above it in years 2 and 3 (output gaps +1.5% and +2.6%) then falls below it in year 4 (-3.9%), year 5 (-5.0%) and year 6 (-2.8%), showing a boom followed by a recession and recovery.
caption: Figure: actual GDP fluctuates around steadily growing potential GDP; the output gap is positive in the boom and negative in the slump

alt: Circular flow of an open economy with the worked-example figures (US$ million): households receive factor incomes from firms and spend on domestic output (C); leakages saving 1,200, taxes 1,800 and imports 900 total 3,900 and flow to banks, government and the rest of the world, while injections investment 1,500, government spending 1,700 and exports 800 total 4,000 flow back to firms, so injections exceed leakages by 100.
caption: Figure: the circular flow with leakages (amber) and injections (blue); J exceeds W by 100 so income expands

alt: Consumption and saving functions for C = 40 + 0.8Y: the consumption line starts at 40 when income is zero and crosses the 45-degree line (C = Y) at the break-even income of 200, below which households dissave; the saving function S = -40 + 0.2Y starts at -40 and crosses zero at Y = 200, with slopes MPC 0.8 and MPS 0.2.
caption: Figure: the consumption function against the 45-degree line and the matching saving function, both break even at Y = 200

alt: Economic rent for welders with supply W = 4 + 0.05L and a market wage of US$10: 120 welders are employed; the triangle between the wage line and the supply curve (half of 6 times 120 = US$360 an hour) is economic rent and the area under the supply curve (US$840) is transfer earnings, out of a total payment of US$1,200.
caption: Figure: economic rent (blue) is the area above the supply curve and below the wage; transfer earnings (amber) lie under the supply curve

alt: Consumer equilibrium: with income US$120, X costing US$4 and Y US$6, the budget line runs from 30 units of X to 20 units of Y; the highest reachable indifference curve touches it at 15 units of X and 10 of Y, where the slopes are equal (MRS = price ratio 0.67); a dashed line shows the pivot to 60 units of X when the price of X falls to US$2.
caption: Figure: the consumer chooses the point where the budget line is tangent to the highest indifference curve (illustrative preferences XY = 150)

alt: Income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of X from US$4 to US$2: the consumer moves from A at 15 units of X to the compensated bundle B at 21.21 units on the original indifference curve (substitution effect +6.21), then to C at 30 units on a higher curve (income effect +8.79), a total price effect of +15 units.
caption: Figure: the dashed line parallel to the new budget line and tangent to the original curve separates the substitution effect (A to B) from the income effect (B to C)

alt: J-curve: after a depreciation the trade balance first worsens from a deficit of US$100 million to US$140 million in quarter 1, then improves to -120, -60, a surplus of +10 in quarter 4 and +40 in quarter 5, tracing a J shape.
caption: Figure: the J-curve, where the trade balance worsens before it improves

alt: Kinked demand curve at 100 units and US$10: demand above the kink is elastic (PED -4) and below it less elastic (PED -1.5); the marginal revenue curve has a vertical gap from US$3.33 to US$7.50 at 100 units, so marginal cost of US$4 or US$7 still gives the same price and output.
caption: Figure: the kinked demand curve and the gap in MR; cost changes within the gap leave price at US$10

alt: Straight-line demand P = 20 - 0.1Q: elasticity falls down the curve, from PED -9 at US$18 and 20 units, through exactly -1 at US$10 and 100 units, to -0.11 at US$2 and 180 units; demand is elastic above US$10 and inelastic below.
caption: Figure: on a straight-line demand curve PED changes from point to point, equalling -1 at the mid-point

alt: Total revenue for the demand curve P = 20 - 0.1Q is an arch: it rises from US$360 at 20 units to a maximum of US$1,000 at 100 units, where PED is -1, then falls to US$360 at 180 units, so revenue is highest at the elasticity of exactly 1.
caption: Figure: total revenue peaks where PED = -1 (100 units, US$10)

alt: Lorenz curves for the quintile data: before, the curve passes through (20, 5), (40, 15), (60, 30) and (80, 55) with the shaded area between it and the line of equality equal to 0.19 so Gini = 0.38; after progressive taxes and transfers the amber curve lies closer to the diagonal at (20, 8), (40, 20), (60, 37), (80, 61) and Gini falls to 0.296.
caption: Figure: Lorenz curves before (blue) and after (amber) redistribution; the nearer the diagonal, the lower the Gini coefficient

alt: Long-run average cost for the bakery's six scales: LRAC falls from US$50.00 at 100 units to a minimum of US$32.26 at 620 units (the minimum efficient scale), then rises to US$35.71 at 700 and US$41.67 at 720 units because of diseconomies of scale.
caption: Figure: the bakery's long-run average cost falls (economies of scale) to 620 units and rises after (diseconomies)

alt: Two schematic aggregate supply curves: the classical long-run curve is a vertical line at potential output; the Keynesian curve has three sections, flat when there is much spare capacity, rising as the economy nears capacity and vertical at full employment. Drawn for illustration, not from data.
caption: Figure: schematic classical (vertical) and Keynesian (three-section) long-run aggregate supply

alt: Demand for maize meal: D1 slopes down from 3 bags at US$5 to 25 bags at US$1; a rise in income shifts the whole curve right to D2, 4 bags more at every price, so at US$3 quantity demanded rises from 12 to 16 bags.
caption: Figure: an increase in demand shifts the curve right from D1 to D2 (4 more bags at every price), unlike a price fall which moves along D1

alt: Market for maize meal: demand Qd = 165 - 15P and supply Qs = 15P - 15 cross at US$6 and 75 thousand bags; at US$4 demand 105 exceeds supply 45, a shortage of 60, and at US$8 supply 105 exceeds demand 45, a surplus of 60, so price moves toward US$6.
caption: Figure: equilibrium at US$6 and 75 thousand bags; below it there is a shortage, above it a surplus

alt: Shifts in the maize meal market from equilibrium E1 at US$6 and 75: a demand increase to D2 gives E2 at US$7 and 90, a supply decrease to S2 gives E3 at US$7 and 60, so the same price rise comes with a rise in quantity if demand shifts and a fall if supply shifts.
caption: Figure: a rightward demand shift (E2) and a leftward supply shift (E3) both raise price, but quantity rises in one case and falls in the other

alt: A maximum price of US$30 below the equilibrium of US$40 and 200 tonnes: quantity demanded is 300 tonnes but only 100 tonnes are supplied, a shortage of 200, and at 100 tonnes buyers would pay up to US$50, so a black market can exceed the original equilibrium price.
caption: Figure: a maximum price below equilibrium creates a shortage (red bar) and an incentive for black-market trade

alt: A minimum price of US$50 above the equilibrium of US$40 and 200 tonnes: quantity demanded falls to 100 tonnes while quantity supplied rises to 300, a surplus of 200 tonnes that the government would have to buy at a cost of US$10,000 to hold the price.
caption: Figure: a minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus (red bar) that must be bought, stored or exported

alt: Minimum wage in a competitive labour market: demand W = 14 - 0.02L and supply W = 2 + 0.01L meet at US$6 and 400 workers; a minimum wage of US$7 cuts the number demanded to 350 while 500 want jobs, so employment falls by 50 and unemployment is 150.
caption: Figure: a minimum wage above equilibrium reduces employment and creates unemployment of 150 (the red bar)

alt: Long-run equilibrium of the salon: entry shifts demand left to P = 30 - 2Q, so MR = MC at 5 customers and price US$20, which equals ATC (10 + 50/5); the demand curve just touches the ATC curve, so profit is normal, and at that output ATC is still falling.
caption: Figure: in the long run entry shifts demand left until it is tangent to ATC at the MR = MC output: normal profit only

alt: Short-run equilibrium of the salon with demand P = 34 - 2Q and MC US$10: MR = MC at 6 customers, price US$22 against ATC US$18.33, a supernormal profit rectangle of US$22 a day.
caption: Figure: in the short run a monopolistically competitive firm earns supernormal profit (green) at MR = MC

alt: Monopoly equilibrium for the quarry with demand P = 80 - 2Q and MC US$20: MR = MC at 15 thousand units, price US$50, with supernormal profit of US$200 thousand (ATC 36.67); a competitive industry would produce 30 thousand at US$20, so the deadweight loss triangle is 225.
caption: Figure: a monopolist sets MR = MC (15, US$50), earns supernormal profit (green) and causes a deadweight loss (red) against the competitive output of 30

alt: Monopsony: with MRP = 14 - 0.02L, labour supply W = 2 + 0.01L and marginal cost of labour MCL = 2 + 0.02L, the employer hires 300 workers where MRP equals MCL (US$8) but pays only US$5 from the supply curve, below the competitive wage of US$6 and employment of 400.
caption: Figure: a monopsonist hires where MRP = MCL and pays the lower wage read from the supply curve

alt: The farm's demand for labour is its MRP curve: with crates at US$4 the MRP falls 64, 56, 48, 40, 32 for the first five workers, so at a wage of US$36 it hires 4 workers; if the price rises to US$5 the MRP curve shifts right (MRP 80, 70, 60, 50, 40) and the farm hires 5.
caption: Figure: the firm hires up to the worker whose MRP is at least the wage (4 workers); a higher product price shifts demand right (5 workers)

alt: The multiplier process for a US$100 million injection with MPC 0.8: cumulative income rises 100, 180, 244, 295, 336, 369 and so on, each round adding 80% of the last, approaching the limit of US$500 million (multiplier 1 / 0.2 = 5).
caption: Figure: each round of spending adds less; cumulative income approaches the multiplier limit of US$500 million

alt: Regulating the natural monopoly quarry: LRAC = 20 + 250/Q falls throughout; unregulated it sells 15 thousand at US$50, marginal-cost pricing gives 30 thousand at US$20 but a loss equal to the fixed cost of US$250 thousand, and average-cost pricing gives 25 thousand at US$30 where price equals ATC and profit is normal.
caption: Figure: price and output under no regulation, marginal-cost pricing and average-cost pricing for a natural monopoly

alt: Negative externality of production: with MPB = 100 - 0.5Q, MPC = 10 + 0.25Q and an external cost of US$15 a unit (MSC = 25 + 0.25Q), the market produces 120 units at US$40 where MPB meets MPC, but the social optimum is 100 units where MSB meets MSC, so over-production of 20 units causes a welfare loss triangle of US$150.
caption: Figure: with an external cost the market over-produces (120 against 100); the red triangle is the welfare loss

alt: Four schematic demand curves: vertical is perfectly inelastic (PED 0), horizontal is perfectly elastic (PED infinity), a steep line is relatively inelastic and a shallow line relatively elastic, drawn for equal axes scales.
caption: Figure: schematic demand curves showing the range of PED (a straight line's elasticity still changes along it)

alt: Short-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive maize farm at a price of US$36: MC is US$30 at the sixth unit and US$42 at the seventh, so output is 6 units; ATC at 6 units is US$28.33 and the shaded rectangle (36 - 28.33) x 6 is a supernormal profit of US$46.
caption: Figure: a price-taker maximises profit where MC meets the horizontal price line; the rectangle is supernormal profit

alt: The maize farm at three prices: at US$28, the minimum of ATC, it produces 5 units and earns normal profit; at US$24 it also produces 5 units and loses US$20 but covers its variable cost (minimum AVC is US$20); at US$18, below minimum AVC, it shuts down.
caption: Figure: normal profit at P = minimum ATC (US$28), a loss that is still worth bearing at US$24, and shutdown below minimum AVC (US$18)

alt: Traditional Phillips curve from the data: inflation falls as unemployment rises, from 6.0% at 3% unemployment to 4.5% at 4%, 3.5% at 5%, 2.8% at 6% and 2.0% at 8%; the curve is steeper at low unemployment, so the trade-off worsens.
caption: Figure: the traditional Phillips curve shows lower unemployment going with higher inflation

alt: Expectations-augmented Phillips curve with natural rate 5%: holding unemployment at 4% gives inflation 3.5% on the first short-run curve (expected inflation 3%), then each year expectations catch up and the curve shifts up by 0.5, giving 4.0%, 4.5% and 5.0%; the long-run curve is vertical at 5% unemployment.
caption: Figure: keeping unemployment at 4%, below the natural rate, shifts the short-run curve up every year; the long-run curve is vertical at 5%

alt: Positive externality of consumption: with MPB = 94 - 0.5Q, MPC = 10 + 0.25Q and an external benefit of US$12 a unit (MSB = 106 - 0.5Q), the market produces 112 units at US$38 but the social optimum is 128 units at US$42, so there is under-provision of 16 units and a welfare loss triangle of US$96.
caption: Figure: with an external benefit the market under-provides (112 against 128); the red triangle is the welfare loss

alt: Production possibility curve for Zandia, bowed outwards from capital goods 100 and consumer goods 100 at the axes through points A to F; a point inside the curve at 60 and 70 wastes resources, a point outside at 80 and 70 is unattainable, and a dashed curve shows all maxima rising 25% to 125.
caption: Figure: Zandia's production possibility curve (concave, so opportunity cost rises) and an outward shift after a 25% rise in capacity

alt: Third-degree price discrimination by a bus company with marginal cost US$10: MR = MC gives adults (less elastic demand) 10 hundred passengers at US$30, and students (more elastic demand) 6 hundred at US$22; profit before fixed costs is 200 + 72 = 272 hundred dollars against 256 at a single price.
caption: Figure: the same MR = MC rule applied in each market gives the higher price (US$30) to adults and the lower price (US$22) to students

alt: Profit maximisation for the firm in the revenue-curves lesson: the fourth unit has MR US$6 above MC US$5 and the fifth has MC US$7 above MR US$2, so output is 4 units at price US$12; average cost there is US$8.25, giving a profit rectangle of 3.75 x 4 = US$15.
caption: Figure: the firm produces where MC meets MR from below (4 units); the green rectangle is the profit of US$15

alt: Market for South African rand: demand D1 and supply S meet at 6.0 US cents and R400 million; a rise in foreign demand of 125 at every price shifts demand to D2, creating excess demand of 125 at 6.0 cents, so the rand appreciates 8.3% to 6.5 cents with R475 million traded.
caption: Figure: higher foreign demand shifts D1 to D2 and the rand appreciates from 6.0 to 6.5 cents

alt: Revenue curves for a firm facing the demand schedule P = 20 - 2Q: average revenue is the downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue starts at the same price intercept and falls twice as steeply (US$6 against AR US$12 at 4 units), reaching zero between 5 and 6 units where total revenue peaks.
caption: Figure: AR (the demand curve) and MR; MR lies below AR and cuts the axis where total revenue is greatest

alt: Short-run cost curves for the bakery with fixed cost US$60: AFC falls throughout, AVC is lowest at 4 units (US$28), ATC is lowest at 5 units (US$40.20), and MC (US$22 at 4 units, US$29 at 5, US$41 at 6) cuts AVC and then ATC from below at their minimum points.
caption: Figure: AFC, AVC, ATC and MC for the bakery; MC cuts AVC and ATC from below at their lowest points (MC is plotted at each unit)

alt: SRAS shifts right by 600 at every price level when costs fall: SRAS1 gives 10,500 at a price level of 100 and SRAS2 gives 11,100; both curves steepen as output approaches potential output of 12,000, where the vertical LRAS stands.
caption: Figure: lower costs shift SRAS right (600 more at each price); both curves steepen towards potential output, shown by the vertical LRAS

alt: A subsidy of US$3 per unit shifts supply down to S + subsidy: equilibrium moves from 500 units at US$14 to 575 units at US$12.50; consumers pay US$1.50 less and producers receive US$15.50, US$1.50 more, at a cost to government of 1,725 with a welfare loss triangle of 112.50.
caption: Figure: a US$3 subsidy shifts supply down; output rises to 575, consumers and producers share the benefit equally and the red triangle is the welfare loss

alt: Effect of a successful supply-side policy: SRAS shifts right by 150 at every price level from SRAS1 to SRAS2, moving equilibrium from real GDP 900 at a price level of 120 to real GDP 950 at 110, so output rises 5.6% while the price level falls 8.3%.
caption: Figure: a rightward shift of SRAS raises output (900 to 950) and lowers the price level (120 to 110)

alt: Equilibrium at US$7 and 100 units with demand P = 12 - 0.05Q and supply P = 2 + 0.05Q: consumer surplus is the triangle between demand and the price line, half of 5 times 100 = 250; producer surplus is the triangle between price line and supply, 250; total surplus 500.
caption: Figure: consumer surplus (blue) lies below demand and above the price; producer surplus (amber) lies above supply and below the price

alt: A maximum price of US$5 on the same market: only 60 units are supplied while 140 are demanded (a shortage of 80); consumer surplus 330 plus producer surplus 90 totals 420 instead of 500, so the triangle of deadweight loss between 60 and 100 units is 80.
caption: Figure: a maximum price of US$5 cuts trade to 60 units and creates a deadweight loss of 80 (red triangle)

alt: Tariff on a small country's imports: world price US$50, domestic demand P = 120 - Q and supply P = 20 + Q; a US$10 tariff raises the price to US$60, cuts quantity demanded from 70 to 60 and raises home supply from 30 to 40, so imports fall from 40 to 20; producers gain 350, the government collects 200, consumers lose 650 and the two triangles are a welfare loss of 50 each.
caption: Figure: a tariff raises the domestic price; producer gain (amber), tariff revenue (blue) and two welfare-loss triangles (red) account for the consumers' loss of 650

alt: A specific tax of US$4 per unit shifts supply up from S to S + tax: equilibrium moves from 500 units at US$14 to 400 units at US$16; consumers pay US$2 more and producers keep US$12, US$2 less, so the burden is split 800 each of the 1,600 revenue, and the small triangle is a deadweight loss of 200.
caption: Figure: a US$4 specific tax shifts supply up by the tax; the revenue rectangle (blue plus amber) is shared equally and the red triangle is the deadweight loss

alt: Supply of tomatoes: S1 slopes up from 3 crates at US$1 to 35 at US$5; lower costs shift supply right to S2 (6 more crates at every price, 24 at US$3) and higher costs shift it left to S3 (2 fewer at every price, 16 at US$3).
caption: Figure: lower costs shift supply right (S1 to S2), higher costs shift it left (S1 to S3)

alt: Zandia's production possibility curve joins 60 tonnes of maize to 30 tonnes of cotton; specialising in cotton and trading at 3 maize per cotton gives a trading possibility curve out to 90 tonnes of maize, outside the PPC, so Zandia can consume 15 maize and 25 cotton (point B) instead of 12 and 24 (A); Mbira's flatter PPC runs from 40 maize to 10 cotton.
caption: Figure: trade lets Zandia consume beyond its PPC; the dashed trading possibility curve lies outside it

alt: Total and marginal utility of bread slices: total utility rises 10, 18, 24, 28, 30 and peaks at 30 for the 5th and 6th slices, while marginal utility falls 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0 and becomes -2 at the 7th slice, where total utility falls to 28.
caption: Figure: marginal utility diminishes; total utility is greatest when marginal utility reaches zero and falls once it is negative
